text: You're given a list of intervals. Return the minimum number you need to remove so that the rest don't overlap. Intervals that only touch at one point, like one to two and two to three, don't count as overlapping.
Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I only return the count, not which ones to remove? And is the input sorted in any way?
Just the count. And no, the input can be in any order.

Okay. One thing I want to say early: removing the fewest is the same as keeping the most. If I can find the largest set of non-overlapping intervals, the answer is n minus that size. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to ten to the fifth intervals, with values between negative fifty thousand and fifty thousand.

Got it. So I need something around n log n. Let me check the examples. One to two, two to three, three to four, one to three: I can keep the first three, since they only touch, and remove one to three, so one. Three copies of one to two: keep one, remove two. One to two and two to three: they touch, so zero. All match.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would try every subset, which is exponential. A dynamic programming version, like a longest increasing subsequence, works but is quadratic, too slow for ten to the fifth. This problem reminds me of the activity selection pattern, a greedy exchange argument. To keep the most intervals, I always keep the one that ends earliest, because it leaves the most room for everything after it.
Why sort by the end and not by the start?

Because starting early doesn't mean getting out of the way early. Take one to ten, two to three, and four to five. Sorted by start, one to ten comes first, I keep it, and it blocks the other two, so I'd remove two. Sorted by end, I keep two to three and four to five and remove only one to ten. The scary part is that the start-sorted version passes all three official examples. I checked it on about a hundred and eleven thousand small cases, and it fails over eleven thousand of them.

Here's the plan, in three steps. Sort by end. Walk through the intervals, and keep one whenever it starts at or after the end of the last one I kept. Return the total minus the number I kept. One thing worth flagging — there are two comparisons, and they're different. The sort comparator must be strictly less than. The keep condition is less than or equal, because touching is allowed.

Alright. I sort with a lambda that returns whether a's end is less than b's end. Then one loop: if my kept list is empty, or its last end is at most the current start, I keep it. I return the size difference. The easy line to get wrong is the comparator. If I write less than or equal there, the comparison isn't strict anymore. With sixteen identical intervals it still works, but with seventeen it crashes with a segmentation fault. I also take the parameters by reference; passing them by value made the sort about nine times slower on ten to the fifth intervals.

Let's dry-run one to ten, two to three, four to five, three to six, six to eight. Expected two. Sorted by end, one to ten goes last. The moment that matters is three to six: the last kept interval ends at five, and three is before five, so it's removed. Its end, six, is later than five, so keeping it would only block more. One to ten is removed at the end too. Corner cases: a single interval returns zero. All identical returns n minus one. A chain that only touches returns zero. Fully nested intervals keep only the innermost.

Let me think about complexity here. Sorting is n log n and the loop is linear, so time is n log n. Space is linear for the kept list, but I only ever look at its last end, so I could keep a single previous-end variable and use constant extra space.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You turned removing the fewest into keeping the most, which made the greedy choice clear. You explained why the end is the right sort key with a concrete counterexample. And you separated the strict comparator from the non-strict keep condition, and knew what breaks when they're mixed up. Good work.
